title: 10ish Instances of People Doing Things Out Of Spite
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck count down a loose top-ten list of examples of people doing things out of spite. They open by clarifying that the phrase "cut off your nose to spite your face" doesn't fit the story of the Coldingham nuns, then cover Henry Clay Frick and Andrew Carnegie's feud, Saddam Hussein's mosaic of George H. W. Bush in the Al Rashid Hotel, Henry Ford II's revenge build of the Ford GT after Enzo Ferrari's deal collapsed (with Ferrari's rebuff of Ferruccio Lamborghini's clutch advice leading to Lamborghini's car company), a spite house-like road in China built around the Luo Bogan household, the Bonn and Beuel "Bridgeman" statue, Bill Ansel's escalating Christmas display in Ross Township, Pennsylvania, Prince's name change to spite Warner Brothers, and the Pink House on Plum Island, Massachusetts. A listener mail segment about currency and Zimbabwe's coin shortage closes the episode.
topics: cut off your nose to spite your face
Saddam Hussein George H. W. Bush mosaic
Chinese house in middle of highway

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the top-ten episode about things done out of spite and the hosts discuss the format.

segments.title: Cut off your nose to spite your face and the Coldingham nuns
segments.summary: Josh explains that the saying does not fit the story of the Coldingham nuns, who mutilated their faces to protect their chastity from Viking raiders in 867 CE and were killed when the Vikings burned the monastery. They discuss the meaning of the saying and an invented saying about hatred.
topics: cut off your nose to spite your face

segments.title: Frick and Carnegie feud
segments.summary: Henry Clay Frick and Andrew Carnegie fell out as steel partners. Frick kept taunting Carnegie and built a bigger mansion nearby. On his deathbed Carnegie sent a conciliatory letter, which Frick rejected. The hosts then briefly discuss Mary Tyler Moore Show recommendations.

segments.title: Saddam Hussein's mosaic of George H. W. Bush
segments.summary: Saddam Hussein placed a mosaic of George H. W. Bush in the entrance of the Al Rashid Hotel in Baghdad so guests would walk over it. After the 2003 invasion, the mural was reportedly smashed and replaced with a portrait of Saddam.

segments.title: Ford versus Ferrari and the Ford GT
segments.summary: After a deal for Ferrari collapsed when Enzo Ferrari rejected Ford's bureaucracy, Henry Ford II built the Ford GT, which beat Ferrari at Le Mans in 1966 and won in later years. A 1966 original was sold for about $6.75 million to a private owner in Jacksonville, Florida. The hosts discuss the Le Mans 24 Hours race.

segments.title: Lamborghini founded out of spite
segments.summary: Ferruccio Lamborghini, a tractor maker with a Ferrari, offered Enzo Ferrari advice on a clutch problem and was rebuffed. He founded Lamborghini in 1963 with former Ferrari workers. The hosts discuss Ferrari and Lamborghini cars and the Magnum P.I. Ferrari.

segments.title: House in the middle of a Chinese highway
segments.summary: Luo Bogan and his wife refused to leave their five-story house in China in 2012 when a highway was built. The road curved around the house, which kept electricity, and they stayed in it to protest inadequate compensation under eminent domain.
topics: house in the middle of highway

segments.title: Bonn and Beuel Bridgeman statue
segments.summary: Bonn paid for a Rhine bridge that Beuel had agreed to share costs on. The city placed a statue of a man mooning Beuel on the bridge, which became a local icon and was visible from Beuel. Bonn charged a fee to cross the bridge to see it. The original was damaged in WWII and later destroyed by youths in 1996; a replica now stands.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Host teases upcoming segments and a sponsor break.

segments.title: Bill Ansel's Ross Township Christmas display
segments.summary: Electrician Bill Ansel put up a huge Christmas light display in his cul-de-sac home in Ross Township, Pennsylvania, which neighbors complained about. After being cited and ordered to take it down, he set up a spiteful replacement display with insulting signs that stayed up year round for years.

segments.title: Prince's name change to spite Warner Brothers
segments.summary: Prince changed his name to an unpronounceable symbol in 1993 in a dispute with Warner Brothers Records over his contract, which limited his release frequency and gave the label song rights. The name change was widely seen as spite; the media referred to him as the artist formerly known as Prince. The contract expired around 2000. The hosts share memories of his concerts.

segments.title: The Pink House on Plum Island
segments.summary: A spite house built in 1925 on Plum Island, Massachusetts, by a man whose ex-wife demanded an exact duplicate of their house after divorce. The house was inhabited until 2011 and later bought by the Parker River National Wildlife Refuge. The hosts define spite houses and note their history in America.

segments.title: Listener mail on Zimbabwe currency
segments.summary: A listener named Tree writes about Zimbabwe's coin shortage after adopting the US dollar, when importing metal coins was too expensive, and suggests it for an episode on currency. The hosts recall Zimbabwe's hyperinflation.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to email feedback and close the episode.
